LESSON 6 OF 12·Injection, XSS & Client-Side Defenses

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Contexts & CSP

Learn how reflected and stored XSS execute scripts in a victim’s browser, why output context matters, and how Content Security Policy reduces impact.

Beginner25 min
Why this matters

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) happens when an application includes untrusted data in a web page without proper encoding or validation for the specific browser context where it appears. When a victim’s browser renders the page, it executes the injected JavaScript within the origin of the trusted site—allowing the script to read page data, make authenticated requests, or alter the UI.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Tracing how untrusted strings reach browser rendering sinks and how context-aware encoding neutralizes execution.

01 User Content
Safe text node
02 Template Renderer
Allowed
03 Browser DOM
  1. Source: User submits profile text, search query, or URL fragment.
  2. Boundary: Application places the value into a template or DOM text property.
  3. Sink: Browser renders readable text without creating new script elements.
01 Markup / Event Payload
Unencoded sink
02 Raw HTML Sink
Unblocked
03 Script Execution
  1. Source: Attacker supplies HTML tags, event attributes, or a javascript: URL.
  2. Boundary: Value is written raw via innerHTML or unescaped template interpolation.
  3. Sink: Browser parser executes injected script inside the victim's origin and session.
01 Untrusted Input
Encoded + restricted
02 Context Encoder + CSP
Verified
03 Inert DOM Text
  1. Source: Untrusted input arrives from the request, storage, or URL.
  2. Boundary: Output is encoded for the exact context (textContent / safe HTML sanitizer) and guarded by CSP.
  3. Sink: Browser displays literal characters; inline script execution is blocked.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • In reflected XSS, untrusted input from the current HTTP request (such as a search query) is echoed immediately into the HTML response.
  • In stored XSS, untrusted input (such as a comment, profile bio, or support ticket) is saved on the server and rendered later to other users or administrators.
  • Each output location in a document—HTML body text, HTML attribute, URL attribute (href/src), or inline JavaScript—is parsed differently by the browser.
  • Context-aware output encoding converts characters that have special meaning in that specific context into safe literal representations before the browser parses them.

The background

Coined in the early 2000s as "cross-site scripting" to describe loading scripts across domains, XSS quickly became the most common vulnerability reported in bug bounty programs worldwide.

Real-world examples

  • Stored XSS in customer support dashboards or admin panels can silently compromise privileged staff sessions when they view an attacker-submitted record.
  • HTML entity encoding inside an href="javascript:..." attribute does not stop script execution because the browser decodes attributes before evaluating the URL scheme.

What to look for

  • Identify every place where user-controlled strings are rendered into HTML templates, attributes, or links.
  • Check user-supplied URLs (such as profile website links or avatar URLs) to ensure only http: and https: schemes are permitted.
  • Inspect whether templates disable auto-escaping (for example, raw HTML directives) on user content.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use modern templating engines or UI frameworks that automatically apply context-aware encoding by default.
  • Validate URLs rendered into href or src attributes so only safe schemes (https:, http:, or site-relative paths) are allowed.
  • Set HttpOnly on session cookies so injected JavaScript cannot read raw session identifiers via document.cookie.
  • Deploy a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) that blocks inline script execution and restricts script sources.
